resources.string: The stream wants %1$s Hz, but this screen offers only %2$s Hz and runs at %3$s Hz.
The screen stays at %2$s Hz, not the %1$s Hz asked for: switching would blank it (modes: %3$s Hz).
The screen stays at %2$s Hz, not the %1$s Hz asked for: switching would blank it, and Android does that only when Match content frame rate is allowed in the display settings (modes: %3$s Hz).
The screen stays at %2$s Hz, not the %1$s Hz asked for: the Android refresh rate setting allows up to %3$s Hz.
The screen stays at %2$s Hz, not the %1$s Hz asked for: battery saver limits it.
The screen stays at %2$s Hz, not the %1$s Hz asked for: the device is hot and limits it to 60 Hz.
The screen stays at %2$s Hz, not the %1$s Hz asked for. Android gives no reason (modes: %3$s Hz).
Variable refresh needs Android 16, so the screen runs at its top rate. With a Rubylight PC, it follows the game’s rate where it can switch without blanking.
This screen has no adaptive refresh rate, so variable refresh runs at the top rate. With a Rubylight PC, the screen follows the game’s rate where it can switch without blanking.
The screen shows only %1$d of %2$d FPS: Android is holding it at half the stream’s rate.
This screen mode can’t show HDR, so the stream is in SDR.
HDR was asked for, but the PC sent no HDR video, so the stream is in SDR.
HDR was asked for, but the PC reports SDR. Turn on HDR for the streamed display in Windows.
HDR is on, but the PC sent no mastering data, so brightness may look off.
HDR is on, but this device’s decoder reports a non-HDR output, so colors may look washed out.
This screen shows HDR only as HLG, which “Render through Vulkan” can’t draw, so the stream is in SDR.
This screen shows HDR only as HLG, but the PC sends HDR10, so brightness and colors may look wrong.
%1$s shown as SDR: the display refused HDR from “Render through Vulkan”.
Dolby Vision needs “Render through Vulkan” off, so the stream is HDR10.
HDR10+ is not passed on with “Render through Vulkan” on this Android version, so the stream is HDR10 without it.
Dolby Vision needs HEVC or AV1, so PyroWave streams %1$s.
HDR10+ needs HEVC or AV1, so PyroWave streams HDR10 without it.
This screen shows HDR only as HLG, but the PC sends HDR10 on PyroWave, so brightness and colors may look wrong. Updating the PC’s host adds HLG on PyroWave.
This screen shows HDR only as HLG, but it refused HLG from PyroWave, so the PC sends HDR10 and brightness and colors may look wrong.
This screen took HLG from PyroWave before the stream, then didn’t show the stream as HLG.
